title: The Origins of the Cristiada: Maderismo
author: Felipe Ávila
content:
_This article by[Felipe
Ávila](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Felipe%20%C3%81vila) originally
appeared in the [September 7, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/09/07/opinion/los-origenes-
de-la-cristiada-el-maderismo), Mexico's premier left-wing daily newspaper._

This year marks 100 years since the Cristiada, the armed uprising by a sector
of the Catholic Church and lay Catholics, above all in the country's center-
west, against the Mexican State that emerged from the Revolution. It is worth
recapping that episode.

The Mexican Revolution opened a new stage in the age-old confrontation between
two visions of the nation that runs through Mexico's nineteenth century,
pitting Catholic conservatives against anticlerical liberals. The War of the
Reform and the Restoration of the Republic were a historic defeat for Mexican
conservatives, always backed by the ecclesiastical hierarchy. After the long
truce between the Catholic Church and the government of Porfirio Díaz, the
revolution of 1910 reopened the wounds that had not managed to heal since the
era of the Reform. The collapse of the Porfirian State and the dispute among
the different groups and projects that leapt onto the national stage to impose
their hegemony provoked the resurgence of that old struggle, which went
through various stages and which, at its most acute moment, once again brought
about a civil war whose main theater of operations was the country's center-
west. Once again the liberal project triumphed, establishing in the
Constitution of 1917 the absolute predominance of the secular State and
considerably restricting the legal and political rights not only of the
Church, but also of the country's lay Catholics.

The Maderista revolution was a political and democratic revolution. Madero was
a convinced and consistent democrat, which is why his government was
characterized by political freedom without precedent in the country's history.
That freedom for all groups and political expressions included both Catholics
and Jacobin and Masonic liberals. Nevertheless, the Catholic clergy's fear
that the Maderista revolution would cancel the stage of conciliation and
tolerance—and of violation of the Reform Laws—that they had enjoyed during the
Porfiriato led the Catholic hierarchy, headed by the Archbishop of Mexico José
Mora y del Río, to organize for the first time—and, ultimately, the only
time—the National Catholic Party (Partido Católico Nacional, PCN). Supported
by bishops, priests, and clergy, as well as by a distinguished generation of
lay Catholics who, committed to the social question, had linked up with
workers' organizations in some of the country's main cities, the Catholic
Party, formed in May 1911, had spectacular growth and became the second
national political force, behind only the new Maderista party. The PCN took
part in the federal elections in the summer of 1911, in which it supported
Madero for the presidency and Francisco León de la Barra for the vice
presidency, the latter finishing in second place. It also managed to win the
governorship of Jalisco, where it swept the elections, and obtained several
federal and local seats.

The strength of the Catholic Party was confirmed in the 1912 elections, in
which it won the governorships of Jalisco and Zacatecas, the legislatures of
seven states, and several senate seats, and held the second-largest minority
in the Chamber of Deputies. Thus the political organization of Catholics
seemed to consolidate itself as an option that appeared to have overcome the
conservatives' historic defeat in the nineteenth century and that could be
part of the government and the republican institutions of the twentieth
century.

That stage, however, was cut short by the assassination of Madero and the
establishment of the Huertista dictatorship. A sector of the Catholic
hierarchy and of the PCN made the mistake of supporting the coup, a coalition
of counterrevolutionary conservative groups that included former Porfiristas,
Reyistas, anti-Maderistas, and Catholics. In fact, the PCN formed part of
Victoriano Huerta's first cabinet and, from the government and the legislative
rostrum, helped legitimize the Huertista dictatorial government which,
nonetheless, soon broke with its allies and was left governing alone under a
state of exception sustained basically by the military. While one sector of
the PCN refused to collaborate with Huerta and was persecuted by him—including
the party's president, Gabriel Fernández Somellera, and Enrique Zepeda,
director of the Catholic newspaper La Nación—the majority of the party did
collaborate, as did the main Catholic hierarchs.

Given what happened afterward, one could argue that the support for Huerta was
one of the greatest historical errors of the clergy and the lay Catholics who
were trying to recover the leading role and the legal and political rights
they had lost with the Reform Laws. And although, when they decided to support
Huerta in February 1913, they could not know that his attempted conservative
restoration would be a resounding failure and that it would be swept away by a
new phase of the revolution, it must also be considered that the conservatism
of the hardest-line sectors of the hierarchy and of lay Catholics was
identified with halting the revolution and restoring their privileges. In
practice, the values and interests of that Catholic sector of the Mexican
right form a core part of the conservatives' vision of the nation, one with a
line of continuity running from the royalist army and the viceregal
authorities that fought against Mexico's Independence, that sustained
Iturbide's empire, the centralist republic, and the dictatorship of Santa
Anna, that opposed the Constitution of 1857 and confronted the liberals in the
Wars of the Reform, and that supported Maximilian's empire and Porfirio
Díaz—and, consequently, supported Huerta as well.

    Felipe Ávila is Director of the National Institute for Historical Studies of the Mexican Revolutions (INEHRM).
